Eggs of the Lesser prairie chicken (Tympanuchus pallidicinctus) incubated at a constant temperature of 34 °C [T = 34 °C] exhibit an incubation period of approximately 23 days [ab = approximately 23 days], a duration broadly comparable to that of other prairie grouse species. Upon hatching, the newly emerged chicks are precocial, and their initial wet weight averages about 15.5 grams [Wwb = about 15.5 grams]. This neonatal mass, while modest, provides sufficient yolk reserves to sustain the chick during the critical first few days of life as it learns to forage. The rate of early growth is rapid, with individuals typically achieving the capacity for flight, or the fledging stage, very soon after emergence. In the field, fledging is often observed to occur one day after hatching [tx = one day after hatching], although this can vary slightly with local conditions and predation pressure at a temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. This extremely short nestling period is a hallmark of the species' ground-nesting, precocial life history strategy, allowing the brood to quickly leave the vulnerable nest site in search of cover and food.

Females typically produce a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], and each clutch contains between 10 and 14 eggs [N_R_i = each clutch contains between 10 and 14 eggs], though the upper end of this range is more common during years with ample spring rainfall. Under optimal thermal conditions, often recorded at a body temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C], the maximum reproductive rate reflects this singular annual effort, resulting in an annual output of up to 14 eggs per year [Ri = up to 14 eggs per year]. Sexual maturation in this species is a relatively extended process; most individuals do not attain puberty until they are 70 days after hatching [tp = 70 days after hatching], which is the approximate time it takes for a juvenile to reach about 90 percent of its adult body mass at a temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. This delay is necessary to build the substantial somatic reserves required for the energetically demanding displays of the breeding lek. Young birds hatched late in the season may even defer growth completion until the following spring, though the 70-day benchmark remains the standard for those hatched under favorable conditions.

The ultimate wet weight achieved by adult females is typically around 719 grams [Wwi = around 719 grams], a mass that reflects significant energetic investment in egg production and brood rearing. Males, in contrast, are considerably larger and more robust, with documented specimens reaching an ultimate wet weight of 789 grams [Wwi = 789 grams]. This pronounced sexual size dimorphism is a common feature among lek-breeding grouse, where larger males have a distinct advantage in male-male competition for central display territories on the lek. Field measurements of body mass taken during the winter months, when fat reserves are at their peak, show that both sexes often exceed these average figures, with some individuals reaching over 800 grams. However, the values of 719 grams for females and 789 grams for males represent the typical asymptotic mass for reproductively active adults in optimal range habitat.

Under the typical active metabolic conditions of an adult bird, which correspond to a core body temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C], the time since birth at first brood production is generally one year. An individual hatched in late spring will not contribute to the next generation until the following breeding season, meaning that first reproduction occurs at approximately 365 days after hatching [tR = approximately 365 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. This is an entire year dedicated to growth, survival over the first winter, and learning the complex social and spatial dynamics of the lek system. The high temperatures required for egg development and chick rearing make the timing of this first brood critical; a female that delays her first nesting attempt risks losing her clutch to heat stress or having insufficient time to fledge her young before autumn. Consequently, the 365-day interval represents a tightly constrained life-history schedule.

Maximum longevity in the wild is considerable for a bird of this size, with the oldest known individuals surviving just over 13.5 years [am = 13.5 years] in the absence of heavy predation or habitat fragmentation at a temperature of 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. This substantial lifespan, maintained when core body temperature is at an active metabolic state of 41 °C [T = 41 °C], allows for multiple reproductive attempts over a lifetime, helping to buffer against periodic poor breeding seasons caused by drought. However, the high metabolic cost of lekking behavior means that many males do not survive to this extreme age, with the average life expectancy being considerably shorter. The 13.5-year record is consistent with that of other long-lived tetraonids and highlights the species' potential for a slow life history when environmental conditions are stable and suitable habitat is continuous.
